content: Ringworm, also referred to as Tinea, is a fungal infection of the skin. It manifests as a reddish to brownish raised or bumpy patch of skin, often lighter in the center, creating a ring-like appearance. Despite its name, ringworm is not caused by a worm but by parasitic fungi, specifically dermatophytes. These fungi feed on keratin, a protein found in the outer layer of skin, hair, and nails. They thrive in warm, moist, and dark environments. At any given time, up to 20% of the population may have a dermatophyte infection. Ringworm is highly contagious and can spread through direct skin-to-skin contact or by touching contaminated objects such as hairbrushes, clothing, or surfaces like toilet seats. It is particularly common in children and individuals who participate in contact sports, such as wrestling. Domestic animals, including dogs, cats, and farm animals, are also frequent carriers of ringworm, and humans can contract the infection through close contact with these animals. Some animals, such as cats, may carry the fungus without showing symptoms. Certain individuals, such as those with eczema or other skin conditions, are more susceptible to ringworm due to a compromised skin barrier. Children are particularly vulnerable before puberty, and some people may have a genetic predisposition to the infection. The hallmark symptom of ringworm in humans is the development of one or more red, raised, itchy patches with well-defined edges. These patches often have a lighter center, resembling a ring. When the scalp or beard area is affected, bald patches may appear. The infection can cause intermittent itching. Physicians can often diagnose ringworm based on its appearance, but they may also take a skin scraping or examine plucked hairs under a microscope to confirm the presence of fungal elements. In some cases, the fungi may fluoresce under a black light. In animals, ringworm typically causes scaling and hair loss, though some animals may show no symptoms. Occasionally, ringworm can trigger skin lesions in areas of the body distant from the primary infection site. These lesions, known as dermatophytids, are fungus-free and represent an allergic reaction to the infection. They usually resolve once the primary infection is treated. Treatment for ringworm typically involves the use of topical antifungal medications, such as miconazole, clotrimazole, terbinafine, butenafine, or tolnaftate. Many of these treatments are available over the counter. For scalp infections, shampoos containing pyrithione zinc, such as Head and Shoulders, can be effective. In children, oral antifungal medications like terbinafine granules may be prescribed to treat scalp ringworm (Tinea capitis). Itching, burning, and scaling associated with the infection can sometimes hinder treatment, and hydrocortisone creams may be used to reduce inflammation and speed recovery. However, fungal infections can take time to resolve, with improvement typically seen within one to two weeks. Infections involving the nails or scalp are more challenging to treat due to the fungus residing in hair follicles or beneath the nails. Griseofulvin is a traditional oral antifungal medication that may be prescribed for stubborn cases, though it can have side effects. In animals, treatments may include sulfurated lime rinses, dilute povidone-iodine washes, or enilconazole rinses. Lufenuron, an ingredient in oral flea treatments, is sometimes used to treat ringworm in pets. Folk remedies for ringworm often involve the use of caustic or acidic substances, herbal poultices, or oils like tea tree oil. However, these remedies lack rigorous clinical testing, and some may cause more harm than the fungal infection itself. Preventing ringworm involves maintaining good hygiene and avoiding conditions that promote fungal growth. To reduce the risk of infection: Avoid sharing clothing, sports equipment, towels, or bedding. Shower and shampoo thoroughly after participating in sports that involve skin-to-skin contact. Wrestlers should inspect their skin regularly, cover infections with protective bandages during practice, and avoid competition until at least one week after symptoms resolve. Gym equipment and mats should be disinfected thoroughly. Wear loose-fitting cotton clothing and change underwear daily. Keep skin clean and dry, ensuring it is completely dry after bathing. Take pets to the veterinarian if they exhibit patches of hair loss, as this may indicate a fungal infection. Continue using topical antifungal treatments for two to four weeks after symptoms have resolved to prevent recurrence.
